questions.q: This lesson's failure checklist lists five recurring categories. Which list matches it exactly?
options: Timeout, partial failure, duplicate delivery, out-of-order delivery, silent data loss
Slow network, bad code, wrong password, server reboot, user error
Only duplicate delivery and silent data loss -- the other categories don't apply to integrations
Timeout, encryption failure, browser incompatibility, DNS failure, license expiration
questions.explain: The lesson's reusable checklist is timeout, partial failure, duplicate delivery, out-of-order delivery, and silent data loss -- a short set of shapes that recur across almost any integration regardless of what systems are involved.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which failure category is Harborline Capital's financial-system integration (Lesson 2) primarily built to defend against, and what is its remaining open risk?
options: Primarily duplicate delivery, defended by idempotency; remaining open risk is silent data loss, addressed by periodic reconciliation
Primarily out-of-order delivery, with no remaining open risk at all
Primarily timeout, with partial failure as the remaining open risk
Harborline's design has no failure risk because Platform Events never fail
questions.explain: Lesson 2's idempotency design directly answers duplicate delivery. The lesson identifies silent data loss -- an event published but never received -- as the remaining open risk, which is why periodic reconciliation matters, not just a working happy path.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say out-of-order delivery is a live risk for Vantage Utilities' external-application case study in a way it wasn't for the first three case studies?
options: Because external callers can fire closely-spaced updates to the same record that a network retry could reorder, which the first three case studies' designs didn't need to account for
Because Salesforce guarantees out-of-order delivery for all internal integrations
Because Vantage Utilities never sends more than one update per day
Because out-of-order delivery is impossible over HTTP
questions.explain: An external caller like the portal can fire rapid successive updates to the same case, and a network retry could deliver them out of sequence -- a risk the lesson flags as more relevant here than in the earlier, internally-controlled case studies.

questions.q: This lesson names one proposed fix for out-of-order delivery in the Vantage Utilities case study. What is it?
options: Disabling all retries so updates are never resent
Either a sequence number the receiving side can check, or treating each update as a full replacement of state so order stops mattering
Requiring the portal to only send one update per customer ever
Switching the entire integration to a nightly batch job
questions.explain: The lesson proposes a sequence number the receiver checks, or the simpler option of treating each update as a full state replacement rather than an incremental change -- either approach removes the dependency on receiving updates in the exact order they were sent.

questions.q: What does this lesson say distinguishes "the integration works" from "the integration fails safely"?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
"Works" describes the happy path; "fails safely" requires a named, deliberate answer to each failure category rather than an assumption that failures won't happen
"Fails safely" means the integration never actually runs
Only batch integrations can ever fail safely; real-time integrations cannot
questions.explain: A walkthrough that only shows data arriving successfully has only been demonstrated, not reviewed. Earning the claim "fails safely" requires a stated, deliberate answer for each of the checklist's failure categories, not silence on what happens when something goes wrong.
